This vignette shows how to describe your own table to DietView. DietView needs
one thing from your data: one row per prey record, that is, one prey taxon
found in one stomach. Taxonomy, tables, figures and dashboards are all built
from that table and from a specification that says which column is which.

```{r setup}
library(DietView)
```

## One row per prey record

Column names are free. You do not rename your data; you declare once which
column plays which role. Here is the example table that ships with the
package. It is invented: 24 prey records from 11 stomachs of three predators.

```{r data}
dat <- read.csv(
  system.file("extdata", "dietview_example.csv", package = "DietView"),
  na.strings = c("NA", "")
)
str(dat)
```

The table has no `kingdom` to `species` columns. DietView adds them when you
attach a taxonomy (see the vignette on WoRMS).

## Declaring roles with `dv_spec()`

```{r spec}
spec <- dv_spec(
  predator       = "predator_species_common_name",
  predator_latin = "predator_species_latin_name",
  stomach        = "stomach_id",
  prey_id        = "aphia_id",       # WoRMS AphiaID, used first when present
  prey_name      = "verified_name",  # scientific name, used when there is no ID
  weight         = "prey_weight",
  digestion      = "digestion_level_id",
  covariates     = c("period", "size_class", "size_bin", "region")
)
```

The roles and what they do:

| Role | Required | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `predator` | yes | the predator of each record; a grouping and display label |
| `stomach` | yes | the stomach each record came from; must be unique across the whole table, because stomach counts count distinct identifiers |
| `prey_id` / `prey_name` | at least one | prey keys used to attach the taxonomy |
| `weight` | no | the weight share (%W) |
| `count` | no | number of individuals per record, for the numerical share (%N). Records without a count contribute nothing to %N, so unidentified material usually disappears from that view |
| `digestion` | no | enables the digestion diagnostic |
| `covariates` | no | columns you want to compare diets across |
| `predator_latin` | no | used to look up identification photos |

## Checking a table against a specification

`dv_validate()` stops if a declared column is missing, if there is no prey key
column, or if a weight is negative. It warns about records with no prey key,
weights that are not numbers and stomach IDs shared between predators, and it
ends with a one-line description of the sample. It reports problems and never
changes your data. It returns the data invisibly, so you can use it in a
pipeline.

```{r validate}
invisible(dv_validate(dat, spec))
```

## Mapping your own survey

To use DietView on another table, write a different `dv_spec()`. If your
columns were `sp`, `stom`, `aphia`, `wt_g` and `yr`, you would write:

```{r own, eval = FALSE}
spec <- dv_spec(
  predator = "sp", stomach = "stom", prey_id = "aphia",
  weight = "wt_g", covariates = "yr"
)
```

The later steps (`dv_prepare()`, `dv_build_tree()`, `dv_sunburst()`,
`dv_build_html()`) read the column names from the specification, never from
your code. The article "Adapting DietView to your own survey" goes through
the other choices you make with a new table.
